My research applies statistical and machine-learning methods to health data, with
an emphasis on prediction from electronic health records and on whether models
built in one setting remain trustworthy in another.

---

## 1. Cross-Country Transfer Learning for ICU Admission Prediction

::: {.project-meta}
In progress · Manuscript in preparation · PLACEHOLDER: start date – present · PLACEHOLDER: lab / advisor
:::

Predicting whether a patient will require admission to an intensive care unit,
using electronic health record data from several countries. The central question
is how far a model trained on one country's records transfers to another, and how
much data from the target country is needed to close the gap that remains.

**Data** — Multi-country electronic health records.
PLACEHOLDER: name the source databases, countries, cohort sizes, and the outcome
definition used for ICU admission.

**Methods** — TabPFN, a prior-fitted transformer for tabular data, as the primary
predictive model, evaluated against PLACEHOLDER: baseline comparators. Training in
a source country with evaluation in held-out target countries, followed by target
adaptation using PLACEHOLDER: adaptation strategy. Sensitivity of the reported
gains to label noise is assessed separately, and results are checked for
reproducibility across repeated splits and random seeds.

**Findings** — PLACEHOLDER: in progress. Add the headline transfer result, the
amount of target data required before adaptation matched a model trained directly
on the target country, and what the label-noise analysis implied.

**Materials** — PLACEHOLDER: GitHub repository · manuscript in preparation

## 2. Deep Neural Networks for Mortality Prediction from EHR Vital-Sign Time Series

::: {.project-meta}
Research project · UNLV summer research program (EIP), Project 4 · Four weeks, June – July 2025 · Team of four ("Deep Patient") · PLACEHOLDER: faculty supervisor
:::

A team research project carried out during a four-week, credit-bearing summer
research program at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, predicting patient
mortality from short sequences of routinely recorded vital signs. The practical
obstacle in this data is that vital signs are not recorded on a regular schedule:
the interval between measurements varies from patient to patient, so the series
must be placed on a common time grid before any sequence model can be applied.
The project was designed around that choice — two interpolation schemes crossed
with two network architectures, compared on the same cohort.

**Data** — Electronic health records from a cancer center in Brazil. Static
features (age, sex, ICU admission status), six vital signs — heart rate,
respiratory rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, body temperature and blood
glucose — observed at five consecutive time points (*t* through *t*−4) for 30
time-varying features, plus delta features encoding the change in each vital sign
between successive points. The outcome was patient mortality, coded as survived
or deceased. After preprocessing, the analysis set comprised 1,682 patients per
class, reshaped to 16,820 × 7 across the five time steps.

**Methods** — Irregular measurement intervals were resolved by interpolating onto
the median observed interval, using either linear or non-linear interpolation.
Each interpolation was paired with a convolutional network and with an LSTM,
giving a 2 × 2 comparison; features were standardized and the classes were
balanced. My assignment within the team was the linear-interpolation + LSTM arm.
Models were compared on F1 score, with accuracy and AUC reported alongside, and
training length was set by the epoch at which validation loss began to rise.

**Findings** — The convolutional models outperformed the recurrent ones on every
metric. The best configuration, a CNN on linearly interpolated data, reached
accuracy 0.773, F1 0.762 and AUC 0.853; the LSTM arms reached accuracy 0.671–0.684,
F1 0.638–0.656 and AUC 0.735–0.744. Interpolation scheme mattered far less than
architecture: within each architecture the two interpolation methods differed by
roughly one point of F1. The comparison is limited to a single cohort, and
external validation on an independent dataset was identified as the necessary
next step rather than completed.

**Materials** — PLACEHOLDER: GitHub repository · presentation slides (internal)

## 3. Digital Cognitive Training Interventions for Dementia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

::: {.project-meta}
Poster · IC-KDA + ASAD 2025 · PLACEHOLDER: date · PLACEHOLDER: location · with Jiyoun Sung (College of Pharmacy, Seoul National University)
:::

A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials asking
whether digital cognitive training — programs delivered remotely through
software, mobile applications or games — improves cognitive and depressive
outcomes in patients with dementia. The protocol was preregistered with PROSPERO
(CRD42025631806).

**Data** — PubMed, Embase and Cochrane, searched under a PRISMA-based strategy for
English-language randomized controlled trials published through December 2024.
Of 466 records identified, 147 duplicates were removed, 319 screened and 22
assessed in full text, leaving 11 studies covering 1,352 participants (636
intervention, 716 control; mean age approximately 83 in both arms). Patients with
mild cognitive impairment or subjective cognitive decline were excluded.

**Methods** — Pooled mean differences under a fixed-effect inverse-variance model,
computed separately for the two outcomes with enough analyzable data: the
Mini-Mental State Examination (4 studies) and the Geriatric Depression Scale
(3 studies). Heterogeneity was assessed with *I*².

**Findings** — Digital cognitive training improved MMSE scores by a mean
difference of 3.94 (95% CI 2.38 to 5.49, *p* < 0.00001) and reduced GDS scores by
1.52 (95% CI −2.68 to −0.37, *p* = 0.01), with moderate heterogeneity in both
(*I*² = 34% and 39%). The evidence base is small — eleven trials, and only three
to four contributing to each pooled estimate — so the effects are best read as
supportive rather than conclusive.

**Materials** — PLACEHOLDER: poster PDF · PROSPERO record CRD42025631806

## 4. Deep Learning-based Neural Granger Causality for Solar Radiation Data

::: {.project-meta}
Poster · PLACEHOLDER: conference name · PLACEHOLDER: date · PLACEHOLDER: location · Department of Statistics, Jeonbuk National University
:::

Classical Granger causality tests rest on a linear vector autoregression, which
limits what they can detect in meteorological series where the relationships are
not linear. This project applied neural Granger causality, following Tank et al.
(2021), to ask which meteorological variables carry predictive information about
solar radiation, and whether the neural formulation recovers relationships the
linear test misses.

**Data** — Hourly observations for Jeonju over the whole of 2023 (8,760 records)
from the Korea Automated Synoptic Observing System: precipitation, temperature,
humidity, solar radiation, wind speed and total cloud cover.

**Methods** — Component-wise MLP and component-wise LSTM models, which fit an
independent network per output variable and read Granger non-causality off the
first-layer weights under a sparsity penalty — sparse group lasso for the cMLP,
group lasso for the cLSTM. A linear VAR at the 0.005 level served as the baseline.
Inputs were min-max scaled, a lag of *k* = 12 was used, and the procedure was
repeated over 50 bootstrap samples so that each candidate relationship could be
summarized by how often it was detected.

**Findings** — With solar radiation as the target, temperature was identified in
every replication by all three methods, and humidity was the next most consistent.
The methods diverged on the variables that behave less like continuous
measurements: precipitation was detected in 37% of replications by the VAR but
79% and 97% by the cMLP and cLSTM, and cloud cover showed the same ordering. The
neural models therefore appear better suited to nonlinear structure in continuous
variables, but the results come from a single lag setting and these models are
sensitive to hyperparameters, so their robustness is not established.

**Materials** — PLACEHOLDER: poster PDF · GitHub repository
